tldr: A challenging task where a quadrotor flies through a swinging narrow gap was achieved purely via end-to-end learning using differentiable simulation, without any teacher data or trajectory planners. Training took only a few minutes on a single GPU to reach a 99.3% success rate in simulation, and achieved an 80% success rate on a real drone using onboard sensors alone.
hero_caption: A physical quadrotor threading through a swinging narrow gap, relying solely on onboard camera and inertial sensor (IMU) information. Direct learning with differentiable simulation achieved zero-shot transfer to the real robot without prior trajectory planning or privileged teachers.
overview:
Flying a drone through a narrow gap at high speed is an extremely difficult task. It demands spatial alignment as well as millisecond-level timing adjustment. When the gap itself moves like a pendulum, the drone must decide not only how to tilt its attitude, but also when to commit to the traversal, using only its onboard camera and gyro information.

With conventional reinforcement learning methods like PPO, learning is exceptionally hard in severe environments where passing through a narrow space means a tiny deviation leads to immediate collision and failure, making reward clues too sparse. Black-box exploration using score-function policy gradients suffers from exploding variance, requiring an astronomical number of trials.

To solve this, the authors built a simulator where the quadrotor's equations of motion and task evaluation functions are fully differentiable. By backpropagating through the physical trajectories inside the simulator (backpropagation through time, or BPTT), they leveraged pathwise gradients. Even from a rollout that collides with the frame and fails, this provides an exact gradient signal indicating in which direction and by how much attitude or timing should be corrected.

With this formulation, training converges in just a few minutes on a single consumer GPU, reaching an astonishing 99.3% success rate in simulation. In real-world experiments, the quadrotor recognized a swinging gate frame lit by LEDs with its onboard camera, successfully traversing it in 8 out of 10 physical trials using only onboard computation, seamlessly bridging simulation and the real world.
contributions: Demonstrated for the first time that dynamic narrow-gap traversal can be learned directly from random initialization, without relying on an expert trajectory planner or distillation from a teacher policy.
Proposed a differentiable moving-gap formulation that smoothly gates alignment and collision costs using the signed distance to the gap plane.
Released an open-source differentiable simulation framework supporting privileged states and onboard visual-inertial observations, converging in minutes on a single GPU.

Theoretically and empirically showed that pathwise gradients overwhelmingly outperform score-function gradients in sample efficiency and convergence on precision-critical tasks with thin feasible manifolds.
Applied the learned visuomotor policy zero-shot to a physical quadrotor, achieving dynamic narrow-gap traversal with an 80% success rate using onboard sensing alone.

sections.heading: Why is threading a moving gap so hard, and what makes this a breakthrough?
sections.summary: Narrow gap traversal is a severe control problem with only a few centimeters of clearance between the drone and the opening. This work proposes an end-to-end approach to solve it directly using differentiable simulation, without teachers or planners.
sections.details:
For drones to navigate quickly through collapsed buildings or confined structures, agile flight skills to squeeze acrobatically through narrow windows or machinery openings are essential. Passing through a static gap already requires millimeter and degree-level precision. When the gap is moving, the difficulty spikes because the drone must simultaneously decide the commitment timing of when to initiate traversal.

Prior approaches have mostly relied on pre-optimized trajectory planners or distilling knowledge from privileged teacher models with full state information into visual models via imitation learning. However, learning from scratch with a randomly initialized neural network without any of these aids was considered extremely difficult.

The fundamental bottleneck lies in the quality of the learning signal. Score-function (SF) gradients used in standard model-free reinforcement learning, such as PPO, treat the environment as a black box. In problems where success lies on a thin feasible manifold, their gradient variance explodes, stalling progress. In contrast, pathwise (PW) gradients utilizing simulator derivatives provide smooth, informative gradients even from failed trials, showing that tilting a few centimeters more to the right would have worked.

The authors formulated smooth geometric costs for a moving gap and built a system that trains in only 0.4 to 5.6 minutes using differentiable simulation on a GPU. This cuts training time by roughly 45x compared to PPO, and successfully transfers to a real quadrotor flying through a moving frame using onboard sensors alone.

sections.heading: Prior drone control and where differentiable simulation fits
sections.summary: Previous narrow-gap traversal studies centered on model-based trajectory optimization or distillation from privileged teachers. This work sets itself apart by targeting moving gaps directly and enabling training within minutes via differentiable simulation without distillation or planners.
sections.details:
### Narrow-Gap Flight Control
Traversing narrow gaps with quadrotors has long served as a benchmark for aggressive flight requiring full $SE(3)$ reasoning. Early works relied on spatial decomposition into convex regions and nonlinear optimization, where even onboard vision setups used manually engineered gap shapes and estimators. Recently, reinforcement learning approaches have emerged, but they still required full state information or a pipeline that distilled model-based planners as teachers.

### End-to-End Visuomotor Policies
End-to-end methods mapping camera images directly to motor commands have advanced, but most demand large-scale imitation learning or massive compute resources. Traversal also poses a severe partial observability issue: right before entering the gap, the frame leaves the camera's field of view, causing blindness. Addressing this has traditionally required complex curriculum learning.

### Emergence of Differentiable Simulation
Making the simulator differentiable to train low-level controllers directly with analytical policy gradients has gained strong attention. While recent work has handled static, irregularly shaped gaps from depth images, this paper explicitly tackles dynamic moving gaps and provides a rigorous mathematical comparison showing why score-function gradients (PPO) fail while pathwise gradients (BPTT) succeed.

sections.heading: Differentiable simulation and the dynamic gap cost formulation
sections.summary: Vehicle dynamics and gap geometry are implemented differentiably in JAX, updating the policy directly via BPTT. A smooth loss gated by the signed distance to a time-varying gap plane turns a sparse traversal event into a dense learning signal.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation and Control Architecture
The drone measures approximately $10\times 38\times 38$ cm, and the rectangular gap measures $25\times 80\times 2$ cm. The quadrotor is approximated as an ellipsoid, and a traversal is counted as a success if its projection onto the gap plane lies entirely within the opening. The gap moves periodically in a pendulum motion.

The control architecture is hierarchical. An onboard low-level controller tracks body rates and thrust at 1000 Hz. The learned policy network $\pi_{\theta}$ runs at 60 Hz, mapping observations to collective thrust $T_t$ and desired body rates $\boldsymbol{\omega}_{\mathrm{des},t}$ (CTBR commands). A one-step communication delay is also modeled.

Two types of observations are considered: (1) privileged state observations containing all relative positions, velocities, and attitudes between the drone and gap, and (2) visual-feature-based observations for the real robot. The visual observation uses no global positions. It takes the drone attitude $\mathbf{R}$ and body rates $\boldsymbol{\omega}$ from the IMU, 2D coordinates of the gap's four corners in camera images, the computed area and aspect ratio, and past action histories.

### 3.2 Differentiable Simulation and Objective Function
Dynamics are integrated using 4th-order Runge-Kutta (RK4), making every step differentiable. Full episode rollouts are unrolled, and gradients are computed directly via backpropagation through time (BPTT).

The core innovation is the design of the per-step differentiable cost $c_t$. It includes gap progress, gap centering, attitude alignment with the frame, smooth collision penalties, and action regularizations. These terms are gated by the signed distance to the time-varying gap plane. As the drone gets closer, geometric alignment requirements intensify, while stabilization terms relax just before crossing. This transforms a sparse traversal event into a smooth, dense pathwise objective.

### 3.3 Training Setup and Domain Randomization
The policy is a compact two-layer Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP with 512 or 1024 hidden units). Training incorporates domain randomization, varying initial positions by $\pm 1$ m, initial velocities, yaw angles, pendulum periods and amplitudes, thrust scaling, and visual feature noise and dropouts.

captions.F3: Overall system pipeline. Actions produced by the policy network are fed to the differentiable quadrotor model to update states. Differentiable costs derived from time-varying gap geometry are accumulated, and their gradients are backpropagated through the computation graph to optimize the policy directly.

sections.heading: Converging in minutes, crushing PPO, and achieving 80% success on hardware
sections.summary: Pathwise gradients exhibited dramatically lower variance than score-function gradients, reaching over 99% success in minutes. Training was 45x faster than PPO, and real flight tests achieved an 80% success rate using onboard sensors alone.
sections.details:
### Pathwise (PW) vs. Score-Function (SF) Gradients
To understand why differentiable simulation works, the authors first compared gradient estimators on toy problems. On non-convex 2D landscapes and slit-passing tasks, SF gradients (the foundation of REINFORCE and PPO) failed to explore and found no gradient even when increasing samples to 4,096. In contrast, PW gradients captured the accurate analytical direction from just a single rollout and converged reliably. While SF gradient variance scales as $\mathcal{O}(T^2)$ with horizon length $T$, PW variance remains bounded at $\mathcal{O}(T)$.

### Simulation Efficiency and Precision
In the quadrotor benchmarks, differentiable simulation achieved 98.9% to 100% success rates on both static and dynamic gaps. Centering error at traversal was just a few centimeters (around 2 cm with privileged state, 7 cm with visual features). Training converged in 0.4 to 5.6 minutes on a single RTX 4080 SUPER.

When compared to PPO with the same 1,000 parallel environments, PPO consumed 19x more transition data and 45.5x more wall-clock training time on the dynamic gap (BPTT converged in ~3.5 minutes, whereas PPO took over 2.5 hours).

### Visual Partial Observability and Real-World Transfer
In the vision-based policy, the gap leaves the camera's field of view (FOV) roughly 0.3 seconds before entry, creating a blind phase. An ablation on observation history length $K$ confirmed that retaining recent frames helps stabilize attitude hold during this blind commitment window.

In physical experiments, a $25\times 80$ cm frame bordered by LED strips swung like a pendulum, and the four detected corner coordinates from an onboard camera were fed to the policy. Across 10 physical trials, the drone achieved clean traversal in 8 runs (80% success rate). In the two failed trials, the drone entered slightly too low and clipped the bottom frame, likely due to unmodeled dynamic or tracking residuals.

captions.F4: Comparison between pathwise (PW) and score-function (SF) gradients. (a) On a non-convex landscape, PW follows the exact gradient in a single rollout, while SF wanders with small sample counts $N$. (b) SF variance explodes quadratically as horizon grows. (c) On a slit-traversal task, SF stagnates even with 4,096 samples, whereas PW learns the solution immediately.
captions.F5: Trajectory snapshots traversing static and dynamic gaps. The quadrotor ellipsoid model accurately aligns its attitude with the aperture of tilted or swinging gaps before passing through.
captions.F8: Onboard camera field-of-view challenge during traversal. As the drone approaches, projected area (blue line) surges, and roughly 0.2 seconds before traversal the frame leaves the FOV completely (red line drops to zero). The policy handles this blind period using past history and IMU measurements.

sections.heading: Summary of achievements, current limitations, and future work
sections.summary: Differentiable simulation proved exceptionally effective for learning precision flight. However, challenges remain for broader real-world deployment, such as reliance on simplified visual features and motion restricted to planar pendulums.
sections.details:
### Summary
This work demonstrated that leveraging low-variance pathwise gradients via differentiable simulation enables end-to-end dynamic narrow-gap traversal in minutes of training, a feat previously deemed impossible without imitation learning or trajectory planners.

### Limitations
- The visual input relies on 4-corner geometric features extracted from LED markers rather than raw RGB images.
- Gap motion was restricted to regular planar pendulum motion, leaving robustness against wind disturbances or irregular 3D motions unverified.
- Real-world evaluation was limited to 10 trials (8 successes), making it difficult to statistically isolate whether the two bottom-frame collisions were caused by perception latency or dynamic tracking residuals.
- As an inherent constraint of BPTT, all simulator components must remain differentiable, and memory and computational costs increase with longer horizons.

sections.heading: Appendix: Mathematical analysis of gradient estimators and real-world vision pipeline
sections.summary: Detailed theoretical analysis on the variance properties of pathwise and score-function gradients, along with the image processing pipeline used to reliably detect gate corners from real camera feeds.
sections.details:
### A.1–A.4 Theoretical Properties of Gradient Estimators
The appendix explores why score-function (SF) gradients break down in narrow-gap tasks. While SF gradient variance scales as $\mathcal{O}(T^2)$ with trajectory length $T$, in stable linear dynamics the Jacobian product norm in PW gradients is bounded by a geometric series, keeping variance at $\mathcal{O}(T)$. Furthermore, in narrow-passage problems, the probability of traversing by random exploration is near zero. Thus, even if batch sizes (parallel environments) are increased to reduce variance, no learning signal exists, rendering SF gradients ineffective.

### Real Gate Detection Pipeline
In physical flights, the green LED frame was extracted from fisheye camera feeds mounted on the drone's front. After HSV color thresholding and noise filtering, quadrilateral contour fitting was performed. The resulting four normalized vertex coordinates were then fed directly into the policy network.

captions.F10: Gate detection pipeline in real-world experiments. From left to right: raw fisheye image, HSV thresholded mask, fitted quadrilateral from contours, and final extracted four corner vertices (red dots).

takeaways: In precision-critical control tasks where success lies on a thin manifold, differentiable simulation (BPTT) vastly outperforms black-box RL (such as PPO).
When dynamics and geometric costs are differentiable, even failed rollouts provide informative gradient directions on how to correct the trajectory.
Cost gating based on signed distance to the passage plane effectively turns a sparse event into a dense, smooth pathwise objective.
With appropriate domain randomization, policies trained in minutes can transfer zero-shot to physical hardware without privileged teachers or complex planners.
limitations: Requires geometric visual features extracted from an LED frame rather than raw pixels, necessitating markers or pre-calibrated transformations.
The gap's trajectory was limited to predictable planar pendulum motion; robustness against sudden movements or non-periodic external disturbances remains unproven.
Physical testing was limited to 10 trials, leaving failure causes (visual perception latency vs. thrust tracking residual) without complete statistical decoupling.
